papers.title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
authors: Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Xintong Li, Nguyen H. Tran, Ken-Tye Yong
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.24381v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. papers.title: KatoANN: Enabling Near-Exact Vector Search at the Speed of Lossy Scans with CPU Matrix Engines
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.27508v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Emerging CPU matrix engines, such as Intel AMX, enable high throughput by batching multiple queries. However, they support only low-precision formats, which can significantly degrade recall (i.e., search quality). We present KatoANN, the first approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search system that achieves both high throughput and high recall simultaneously on CPU matrix engines. Specifically, KatoANN represents each vector using a 16-bit code, splits it into high- and low-byte planes, and computes near-exact distances using 8-bit matrix multiplications that the matrix engine supports. papers.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
authors: Yicheng He, Yuqi Xue, Tianyang Wu, Jian Huang, Bin Hu
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.24733v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. papers.title: PULSAR-V: I/O-Aware Post-Update Attestation for RISC-V
authors: Niccol\`o Lentini, Stefano Di Carlo, Alessandro Savino
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.24135v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Post-update attestation proves that a device installed the intended firmware, not that the image stayed protected until the report was signed. In a multi-master SoC, a master outside the attested processor can corrupt update-critical memory. In contrast, the firmware identity, lifecycle state, and the CPU's protection evidence remain byte-identical to a healthy device's. papers.title: Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation
authors: Ruijie Gao, Jirong Yang, Mengtian Hong, Youyou Lu, Barry Lyu, Haoran Jin, Nathan Bleier
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2608.00894v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Emerging accelerators rarely ship with mature compiler backends, so recent work asks LLM agents to write native kernels directly from ISA documentation and simulator feedback. On two such accelerators, this direct workflow returns a correct kernel on only 17 of 38 workload instances, and most of its inference budget is spent re-deriving machine semantics and repairing illegal code rather than optimizing the workload. We present Contour, which consists of two parts. Contour-Explore replaces native-code generation with search over a mapping surface: a typed set of scheduling knobs and their legal domains, generated automatically from the accelerator's ISA description and the workload graph. papers.title: Programmable Probabilistic Computer with 1,000,000 p-bits
authors: Navid Anjum Aadit, Xiuqi Zhang, Shuvro Chowdhury, Kevin Callahan-Coray, Kyle Lee, Saleh Bunaiyan, Sanjay Seshan, Clayton Thomas, Jason Twigg, Andrew Seawright, Forrest Brewer, Tathagata Srimani, Kerem Y. Camsari
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2606.25313v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Many problems in physics and machine learning require sampling the collective states of large numbers of interacting variables. On modern graphics processors, repeated movement of interaction data between memory and compute units can limit how efficiently these calculations can scale. Here we demonstrate a programmable probabilistic computer with one million interacting probabilistic bits (p-bits) across 18 field-programmable gate arrays, sustaining $10^{12}$ probabilistic updates per second. Coupling weights remain beside the update circuits in on-chip memory, and only single-bit boundary states pass between devices.
